# Mario Peng Lee

> cofounder of condense.chat. making powerful AI accessible to everyone, and safe when it gets there.

I'm cofounder and chief scientist at [condense.chat](https://condense.chat/), which compresses what coding agents send to the model so heavy AI workloads cost less (up to about 70% off long sessions, with basically the same output). I'm also CEO of [Pocketful](https://pocketful.ai/), which brings WhatsApp AI agents to restaurant owners in Argentina. Same mission for both: AI that everyone can actually afford and use.

My background is in linguistics, computer science and psychology (UCLA, Phi Beta Kappa). What I'm most interested in is how minds, human and machine, represent things, and how understanding that makes AI cheaper and safer. These days that means open-source interpretability research at [EleutherAI](https://www.eleuther.ai/).

Before condense I was a senior AI engineer at [nexos.ai](https://nexos.ai/), where I built the agent layer, the memory model behind nexos.heartbeat, and a sandboxed code interpreter.

## writing
- [Where role collapse happens in diffusion models](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/role-collapse.md) (2026-10-23): Prompt SDXL for a mouse chasing a cat and you usually get a cat chasing a mouse. My first suspect was CLIP reading prompts as a bag of words, but after ruling out the encoder, guidance, and cross-attention, the problem seems to sit in the UNet itself.
- [Kids vs LLMs at telling a story](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/kids-vs-llm-stories.md) (2026-10-18): Give a five year old and a language model the same wordless picture book. In 2024 the kids kept track of the characters far better than GPT-4. Two years of models later, the best ones tell the story just like the kids do.
- [cyclediffusion: can a picture be a bottleneck?](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/cyclediffusion.md) (2026-10-17): I trained a diffusion model so a captioner could read its pictures back into the original sentence. Instead of inventing a secret visual code, it collapsed into texture, and the reason is the reader you train against.
- [A transformer that passes the wug test](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/phonetic5.md) (2026-10-16): I fine-tuned T5 to turn spelling into IPA. Nobody told it English phonology rules, but it says "wugs" with a /z/ and "wuks" with an /s/, just like a kid does.
- [Why linguists keep writing about John and Mary](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/diverse-names.md) (2026-10-15): In linguistics papers, 30% of male names are John and 31% of female names are Mary. A good list of names doesn't fix that, because people still pick from it. A random generator does.
- [Do sparse autoencoders capture manifolds?](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/cross-seed-saes.md) (2026-07-15): A concept like "year" lives on a curved manifold, and a single sparse autoencoder often shatters it instead of capturing it whole. Training several SAEs that differ only in random seed and pooling them tiles the manifold back together, right where one SAE dilutes it.
- [block-GRPO: doing RL on a diffusion language model](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/block-grpo.md) (2026-05-09): GRPO needs a log-probability that diffusion LLMs can't give you cheaply. The fix is to use the model's own block-autoregressive structure, and a few bugs later it beat vanilla GRPO by about 10x on tail reward.
- [Building nexos.heartbeat: the infinite context problem](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/heartbeat.md) (2026-03-01): An always-on AI twin doesn't have a context window problem, it has an infinite context problem. Information theory, the design space, and why our memory is a git repository.
- [GPT-2, IOI, and the sphex problem](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/gpt2-ioi.md) (2025-05-21): A wasp can look like it understands what it's doing right up until you move one thing. I poked at GPT-2's indirect-object circuit the same way, to see whether it understood the task or just had a routine that usually works.
- [Does parameter sharing help? a multitask recommender experiment](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/multitask-training.md) (2025-05-10): I built the same recommender four times to find out whether sharing parameters across tasks helps. It turned out the loss weighting mattered more than the sharing, which is a known and slightly annoying axis.
- [Starting a blog](https://mariopenglee.com/blog/hello.md) (2025-05-01): Why this page exists, and what to expect.

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/role-collapse.md -->
---
title: Where role collapse happens in diffusion models
date: 2026-10-23
summary: Prompt SDXL for a mouse chasing a cat and you usually get a cat chasing a mouse. My first suspect was CLIP reading prompts as a bag of words, but after ruling out the encoder, guidance, and cross-attention, the problem seems to sit in the UNet itself.
---

If you prompt SDXL with "a mouse chasing a cat", about three times in four you
get a cat chasing a mouse. The same goes for "a horse riding an astronaut" or
"a doll holding a grandpa": both entities show up, in the roles they usually
have. [Malakouti and Kovashka](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10037) call this role
collapse. I wanted to know which part of the pipeline is responsible, so I went
through the obvious suspects one at a time. My answer so far is that the text
encoder isn't the problem. The denoiser gets the roles and draws the usual
pairing anyway.

The prompts follow their RoleBench setup: 10 relations, each in a common
direction and a rare reversed one, active and passive voice, 4 images per
prompt. A vision-language judge labeled each image correct, reversed, or
neither. On a few hundred images I labeled myself, it sometimes calls a
direction where I'd say neither (so the reversed rates are probably a bit
high), but when it picks a direction it agrees with me.

## suspect one: CLIP

This was my first guess. CLIP is known to treat captions a lot like a bag of
words ([Yuksekgonul et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01936)), and it
reads left to right, so in "a photo of one cat chasing one mouse" the cat token
is computed before the verb exists. A linear probe for the role of the first
noun sits at chance (0.50) in both of SDXL's CLIP encoders. So SDXL really is
getting role-blind noun tokens.

T5-XXL is the opposite. The first noun's role is decodable at about 1.00,
including on relations the probe never saw, and in later layers the probe also
works on sentences like "one mouse that one cat is chasing", which have no
"being" in them. So T5 seems to encode the actual role.

SD3.5-Large uses T5 alongside CLIP, which makes it a clean test. If CLIP were
the cause, SD3.5 should do better. It doesn't:

```
rare prompts, reversed rate
SDXL                       0.74
SD3.5-Large                0.72-0.75
SD3.5, T5 only             0.45-0.57
```

Zeroing the CLIP inputs lowers the reversed rate, but almost all of that moves
to "neither" (a missing lion, a baby held instead of fed). Correct goes up by
about 4 points. When both entities are drawn, they still have the usual roles.

## suspect two: weak conditioning

Maybe the model has the roles but the prior outweighs them, and stronger
guidance would push them through. On SDXL, CFG 3, 7, and 12 all leave rare
prompts 68-74% reversed, and so does passive voice (78%) and IterComp, a
fine-tune trained for composition (76%). The pictures do change between
settings, just not who is doing what.

[[demo:role-collapse-rates]]

## suspect three: cross-attention

Another option is that the noun tokens leak into each other's image regions.
They don't seem to. In reversed images the attention maps for the two nouns
are as separate as in correct ones (top-10% IoU 0.054 vs 0.053). Each noun gets
its own region, and the model draws that entity in its usual pose.

## suspect four: some part of the conditioning

Last, I tried splicing on SDXL: replace the verb, EOS, or pooled embedding with
the one from the role-swapped prompt and see whether the drawn roles follow.
None of these moved the reversed rate by more than about 4 points, which is
within noise. My guess at why comes from comparing the two prompts with no
splicing at all:

```
P(drawn as "A verbs B"), prompt "A verbs B" vs "B verbs A"
common pairs     0.76 vs 0.74
other pairs      0.48 vs 0.45
```

Swapping the whole sentence changes the result by about 3 points. Most of the
outcome is set by which two nouns are in the prompt, so there isn't much role
signal for a splice to find.

## what's left

That leaves the denoiser itself (the UNet in SDXL, the MMDiT in SD3.5). With
T5 the roles are in the text embedding, and SD3.5 draws what's typical for the
noun pair anyway.

That also suggests what to do next. If the failure is inside the UNet, then a
model that does draw reversed roles, like the LoRA from the ReBind paper, should
differ from base SDXL somewhere in there. My plan is to train a
[block-sparse featurizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25234) (BSF, a sparse
autoencoder whose features are small subspaces) on UNet activations from both
models, and look for a block that tracks the reversal. The part I'm most
curious about is whether that block is separate from the ones for the subject
and object. If it is, role would be its own feature in the UNet, something you
could probably steer directly.

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/kids-vs-llm-stories.md -->
---
title: Kids vs LLMs at telling a story
date: 2026-10-18
summary: Give a five year old and a language model the same wordless picture book. In 2024 the kids kept track of the characters far better than GPT-4. Two years of models later, the best ones tell the story just like the kids do.
---

Hand a five year old a wordless picture book and they'll tell you a story:
"a dog finds a paint can, and then he knocks it over, and then he sees a
cat..." The dog stays the dog the whole way through. In 2024, GPT-4 doing
the same task lost track of its characters much more often than the kids
did. Today the best models are indistinguishable from them.

## the setup

With Amalia Ionescu and Catherine Sandhofer at UCLA's Language and Cognitive
Development Lab, we had 31 children aged 4 to 6 narrate *Bow Meow Wow* by
Priya Kuriyan (Pratham Books, CC BY 4.0), a wordless book where a dog tips
over a paint can, meets a cat, and the two end up making a painting. They
went page by page. The models got the same pages, one image per turn, and
told stories of about the same length (115 to 200 words
vs the kids' 154).

To measure how well each storyteller keeps track of characters we used
coreference resolution ([FastCoref](https://github.com/shon-otmazgin/fastcoref)),
which groups every mention of the same entity ("a dog ... he ... the yellow
dog") into a chain. The longer the chains, the more the story keeps coming
back to the same characters instead of losing them.

## the result

Kids averaged 5.66 mentions per character. GPT-4 averaged 3.15, a huge gap
(Cohen's d = 2.2). Then we ran the same book through six models, 30 stories
each, and the gap shrinks with every generation:

```
model                 gap vs kids (d)
gpt-4 (2024)          2.20
gpt-4 turbo           1.85
gpt-5.5               1.75
gpt-6.1 sol           0.94
claude haiku 5.5      0.93
claude opus 5.5       0.42   (not significant)
claude sonnet 5.5     0.33   (not significant)
```

[[demo:kids-gap]]

Opus and Sonnet tell this story with the same referential cohesion as a
four to six year old. No model goes past the kids yet.

## kids and models get there differently

Matching on chain length doesn't mean the stories look alike. Kids lean on
pronouns, "it ... it ... he", sometimes for a character they never actually
introduced: they left about 0.87 pronouns per story that couldn't be tied to
anyone, vs 0.20 or fewer for every model. Models do the opposite, introducing
each character explicitly and then varying how they refer to it ("a fluffy
dog", "the pup"). Same cohesion, different strategy. My guess is the kids
are narrating their own picture of the scene, while the models write for a
reader.

## what's next

Seems to me chain length is a good first measure, and frontier models have
basically caught up on it. The next thing I'd want to look at is whether a
storyteller introduces a character before referring back to it, and whether
the story has real causal structure ("he knocked it over, so the cat ran"),
which is much closer to what we mean by a coherent story. Code and model
outputs are [on GitHub](https://github.com/mariopenglee/llm-child-narratives)
(the children's transcripts stay private).


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/cyclediffusion.md -->
---
title: cyclediffusion: can a picture be a bottleneck?
date: 2026-10-17
summary: I trained a diffusion model so a captioner could read its pictures back into the original sentence. Instead of inventing a secret visual code, it collapsed into texture, and the reason is the reader you train against.
---

If you force a picture to carry a sentence, text to image and back to text,
does the picture stay something a person can read, or does it drift into a
private code only the captioner understands? I trained exactly that loop.
It didn't learn a code. Left alone it collapsed into carpet-like texture,
and the captioner happily described every image as "a man standing in front
of a wall that says 'The Wall'".

## the setup

The idea is an autoencoder whose bottleneck is a picture you can open and
look at, the same instinct as natural language autoencoders
([transformer-circuits, 2026](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/nla/))
but in pixels. It started as a project on relational representations in
visual models at UCLA's Computational Vision & Learning Lab, with Andrew Lee
and Hongjin Lu.

A caption goes into Stable Diffusion
([code](https://github.com/mariopenglee/cyclediffusion)), and a frozen
Pix2Struct captioner scores how likely the original caption is given the
generated image. That score is the cycle loss, and it trains the diffusion
UNet. For the gradient to reach the image I rewrote Pix2Struct's patch
extraction and flattening as pure tensor ops, so the whole loop is
differentiable. A second term, the usual denoising loss on real COCO
image-caption pairs weighted by lambda, ties the model to real pictures, and
lambda=0 is the pure cycle.

## what it learned

Each checkpoint generated images for 200 held-out COCO captions, scored by
the training critic (Pix2Struct), a captioner it never trained against
(BLIP), and CLIPScore:

```
change vs base              p2s_nll   blip_nll   clip
lambda=0, step 500            +0.14     +1.50    -13.0
lambda=1, step 750            -0.22     +0.18     -3.0
LoRA lambda=0.1, step 750     -0.11     +0.10     -1.5
```

With the pure cycle the images turn into carpet and stone-wall textures,
BLIP calls them "a close up of a carpet", and even the critic's own score
gets worse. With the anchor, the critic's score improves while BLIP and CLIP
get worse, so the generator is learning to please one specific reader rather
than to carry the meaning.

[[demo:cycle-critic]]

## the reader is the bottleneck

The reason is the critic. This Pix2Struct checkpoint was fine-tuned on
TextCaps, captions about text inside images, and even on the untouched model's
pictures it describes a kitchen as "a building with a clock that says
10:00". Train against it and the generator inherits that fixation on signs
and shirts that say things.

My takeaway is that a readable bottleneck is only as readable as the reader
you train it against. A narrow critic hands you its biases, and a loop with
nothing anchoring it to real images finds a degenerate picture, not a clever
code. Next I want to swap in BLIP-large as the reader and see whether a
captioner that actually describes scenes keeps the pictures honest.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/phonetic5.md -->
---
title: A transformer that passes the wug test
date: 2026-10-16
summary: I fine-tuned T5 to turn spelling into IPA. Nobody told it English phonology rules, but it says "wugs" with a /z/ and "wuks" with an /s/, just like a kid does.
---

In 1958 Jean Berko Gleason showed children a made-up creature, said "this
is a wug", showed two of them and waited. The kids said "two wugs" with a
/z/ at the end, not an /s/, for a word they had never heard. They weren't
remembering anything. They had learned a rule: the plural is voiced after a
voiced sound and devoiced after a voiceless one, so "bugs" ends in /z/ and
"bats" in /s/.

I wanted to know if a transformer that only ever sees spelling and
pronunciation learns that rule too, or just memorizes a dictionary.

## the setup

The task is grapheme to phoneme (G2P): text in, IPA out. Older G2P systems
are built from rules that linguists write by hand. I didn't give the model
any. I fine-tuned T5 small, base and large (60M to 770M parameters) on
about 113k English word and IPA pairs from ipa_dict, and added the IPA
symbols to the tokenizer so the model could actually write them. That's the
whole training signal: words and how they're pronounced, no phonology.

I also built two English to IPA sequence datasets for future work and put
them on Hugging Face
([ipa_dict_seq2seq](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mariopeng/openIPAseq2seq),
[OpenWebIPA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mariopeng/openwebIPA)).

## the wug test

Then I gave every model words that aren't in the data, built as minimal
pairs:

```
prompt    t5-small    t5-base     t5-large
wuks      [wəks]      [wəks]      [wəks]
wugs      [wəgz]      [wəgz]      [wəgz]
musips    [məsəps]    [mjuzɪps]   [mjuzɪps]
```

All three models pass. "wuks" and "wugs" differ only in whether the
consonant before the s is voiced, and the models flip the plural from /s/
to /z/ exactly where a native speaker does. The s in "wugs" isn't
copied from spelling, because the spelling says s. The model has learned the
rule that turns it into a /z/.

[[demo:wug-test]]

The same thing shows up on loan words. No model would write the /ts/
cluster at the start of "tsunami", because English words can't start that
way. The bigger the model, the closer it got to how a native speaker says
words like "coyote", "chow mein" and "receipt". Scale buys phonotactics the
same way it buys syntax.

## what it means

A speaker's sense of what sounds like English ("brick" yes, "bnick" no)
comes from the words they know, and a model trained on nothing but words
ends up with a piece of the same knowledge. That makes these models a
cheap way to test ideas about how people learn sound rules. Since you can
look inside them, the next step is to find where in the network the
voicing rule lives.

The paper was published in the *UCLA Undergraduate Science Journal*
(2023) as "Transformer Phonotactics via IPA G2P Finetuning"
([preprint](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1UBAq5x_5ZNalz5k98V0eq55oVT-PO4VP/view)),
and you can try the model in the [demo](https://phonetic5.streamlit.app/).

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/diverse-names.md -->
---
title: Why linguists keep writing about John and Mary
date: 2026-10-15
summary: In linguistics papers, 30% of male names are John and 31% of female names are Mary. A good list of names doesn't fix that, because people still pick from it. A random generator does.
---

Open a linguistics paper and look at the example sentences. "John thinks
Mary left." A survey of 927 papers in three major journals found that
30% of all male names were John and 31% of all female names were Mary.
Male arguments showed up twice as often as female ones, and they were the
ones doing things. Textbooks look the same, and they haven't changed much
since the 1990s.

Nobody chooses this. When an example needs a name and you're at a
whiteboard, you reach for the first one in your head, and the first one in
your head comes from the culture you grew up in.

## a list isn't enough

The obvious fix is a curated list of diverse names, and good ones already
exist. But choosing from a list is still choosing. Over a semester the
same unconscious pull comes back, even with a balanced list and good
intentions.

So with Maura O'Leary and Rainey Williams we built the
[Diverse Names Generator](https://diversenamesgenerator.com/), which takes
the choice away. You press generate, or swipe a card in the Android app,
and get a random name from a database linguists curate. The bias never
gets a chance to act.

[[demo:name-draw]]

## making random usable

Random only works if people actually use it in a real classroom, so every
name comes with what an instructor needs at that moment:

- an IPA transcription, so you can say it confidently
- its usual gender association and the languages it comes from
- sometimes a recording, its native script, and famous people who share it

Filters make sure the randomness still fits the example. Semanticists need
one name per first letter so the initials don't collide in logic notation,
syntacticians need to match gender features, and one filter keeps to
English phonotactics for instructors worried about unfamiliar clusters.
Inside those constraints the pick is still random. The app downloads the
filtered set once with a single database call, then generates from that
local list, so it works offline in a classroom with bad wifi and never
shows the same name twice in a row.

The names come from users and students. Phonetics instructors can give
their students credit for submitting a name with a recording, which turns
an IPA exercise into something that ends up in front of other classes.
Linguists check every submission by hand before it goes into the pool.
When we published, the database had over 200 names from more than 30
languages.

## the point

The bias here isn't in anyone's values, it's in which name comes to mind
first. You can't train that away, but you can design it out. When the
default changes, the examples change.

The paper is in the
[*Proceedings of the LSA*](https://journals.linguisticsociety.org/proceedings/index.php/PLSA/article/view/5541)
(2023), and we presented it at the LSA 2023 Annual Meeting.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/cross-seed-saes.md -->
---
title: Do sparse autoencoders capture manifolds?
date: 2026-07-15
summary: A concept like "year" lives on a curved manifold, and a single sparse autoencoder often shatters it instead of capturing it whole. Training several SAEs that differ only in random seed and pooling them tiles the manifold back together, right where one SAE dilutes it.
---

The representation of a year inside a language model isn't a point, it's a
helix: a periodic part (the decade digit) wound around a linear axis (the
century). Color traces a curved surface, days of the week trace a ring. A lot
of concepts are like this. They live on smooth low-dimensional manifolds
rather than single directions, which raises an awkward question for the main
tool we use to read models. A
[sparse autoencoder (SAE)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features)
is built to break an activation into a few discrete atoms, so what does it do
with a continuous curved surface?

Often it doesn't capture it cleanly. That's the finding in Bhalla et al.,
["Do Sparse Autoencoders Capture Concept Manifolds?" (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28119):
instead of allocating a compact group of atoms that span the manifold (they
call this global capture), an SAE tends to shatter it into many atoms that
each tile a small local patch, or land in a fragmented in-between they call
dilution. My follow-up question was simple. SAE training is stochastic, so each
random seed shatters the manifold a bit differently. If you train several SAEs
that differ only in seed and pool their atoms, do the different shatterings
tile the manifold more fully than any single one does?

The short answer from a [small POC](https://github.com/mariopenglee/cross-seed-manifold-poc)
is yes, and the benefit shows up exactly where a single SAE gives up.

## where pooling helps

I used a synthetic benchmark from the paper (48 manifolds, circles and helices
and swiss rolls, placed in a 128-dim space), because the geometry is known and
reconstructions can be scored against ground truth. A manifold's fate is set by
the TopK sparsity `k`. Near `k` equal to the manifold's dimension a single SAE
captures it compactly from a handful of atoms, and pooling adds basically
nothing. As `k` grows the SAE dilutes the manifold across redundant atoms, and
that's where pooling pulls ahead: the gap in a few-atom reconstruction score
grows from about +0.01 at clean capture to roughly +0.1 at deep dilution. So
the benefit tracks dilution. Pooling helps precisely where one SAE stops
capturing the manifold cleanly.

## the intuition, to play with

The demo below is a toy version of the mechanism (not a real SAE, just the
geometry). Pick a helix, sphere, or torus, the kind of shape a real concept
traces, and drag to spin it. Each seed scatters atoms over the manifold, and
each covers a small patch. The score is few-atom capture: how much the best
handful of patches tile, which is what the paper's metric rewards. One seed
leaves gaps, a second seed's gaps land elsewhere, so the pooled panel fills in
where the single-seed panel has holes (turn on "color by seed" to see which
seed covers what). Push the sparsity `k` up into dilution and the gap grows.

The third panel is the tell. It's one SAE as wide as the whole pool, the same
total atoms and compute, and you might expect it to win. But at high `k` it can
fall behind even a single narrow seed. With the same sparsity budget spread
over more atoms, each one specializes to a finer patch, and a few fine patches
tile less of the manifold than a few coarse ones. Widening one SAE shatters the
concept right where pooling separate seeds tiles it.

[[demo:manifold-tiling]]

## tiling, not cleaner copies

The wide control rules out the obvious worry (that pooling just wins on atom
count) since it has those atoms and still loses. The other question is whether
the pool's gain is complementary coverage or just denoised copies of one
solution. I aligned each seed's atoms to a reference and averaged the matched
ones. Averaging can clean up a shared solution but can't invent an atom in a
region no seed covered, and it recovered basically none of the gain (often it
came out worse than a single seed). The pool's improvement also concentrated on
exactly the points the best single seed reconstructed worst. So the seeds tile
complementary regions rather than agreeing on one answer you could average.
Decomposing the gain, roughly half is just having several independent SAEs to
draw from and half is genuine seed diversity.

## what I'd hold loosely

This is toy data with known geometry and one reconstruction metric, and it's a
few-percent effect, not a step change. The reason I think it's interesting is
the reframe: seed variation usually gets filed as instability, but here it
behaves like coverage, and coverage is something you can pool.

The catch is that on a real model you can't score against ground truth, since
you don't know the manifold. So the test I actually care about is next: pool
seeds on Llama-3.1-8B activations for concepts whose geometry we can at least
guess (years, colors, days), and see whether the places the seeds diverge are
where a single SAE was quietly diluting a concept. If pooled-seed agreement can
flag real manifold structure, that's a cheap knob worth having.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/block-grpo.md -->
---
title: block-GRPO: doing RL on a diffusion language model
date: 2026-05-09
summary: GRPO needs a log-probability that diffusion LLMs can't give you cheaply. The fix is to use the model's own block-autoregressive structure, and a few bugs later it beat vanilla GRPO by about 10x on tail reward.
---

GRPO needs one number from your model: the log-probability of the sequence
it just generated. An autoregressive model hands it over for free. A
diffusion language model doesn't, and that single gap is most of the
difficulty in doing RL on one.

GRPO (group relative policy optimization, from DeepSeekMath, Shao et al.
2024) is the workhorse behind a lot of recent reasoning models. You sample a
group of completions, score them, and push the policy toward the
above-average ones, weighted by `log π(sequence)`. The whole method assumes
that log-prob is exact and cheap. On a diffusion LLM it's neither, because
the model defines the sequence through an iterative denoising process, not a
left-to-right product of conditionals, so the exact likelihood is a sum over
denoising paths you can't enumerate.

## what diffu-GRPO did, and where it leaks

The prior work here is d1
([arxiv 2504.12216](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12216)), whose diffu-GRPO
estimates the log-prob with a one-step approximation under random masking. It
works, but the estimate is biased in a way that compounds over training: you
end up optimizing a noisy proxy for the thing you care about, and the noise
isn't mean-zero.

My angle was to stop fighting the model's structure and use it. The target
here, Fast-dLLM v2
([weights](https://huggingface.co/Efficient-Large-Model/Fast_dLLM_v2_7B)),
isn't pure diffusion: it's block-autoregressive. It generates a block at a
time, left to right across blocks, denoising within each block. That
factorization is exactly the handle GRPO wants. The sequence log-prob is
exact across blocks (a real chain rule over the block order) and only needs
approximating within each block. You've shrunk the hard part from the whole
sequence to one block.

[[demo:block-factorization]]

## three estimators for the within-block term

Within a block you still owe an intractable likelihood, so I tried three
ways to approximate it, trading bias for compute:

- **Masked (baseline):** the cheap one-step estimate, kept for comparison.
- **Per-block ELBO (default):** a proper evidence lower bound on the block
  likelihood, averaged over masking levels. More compute than masked, much
  less bias, and it's a bound rather than a point guess.
- **Gauss-Legendre quadrature:** treat the masking-level average as an
  integral and place the evaluation points by quadrature instead of
  sampling. Fewer, better-chosen samples for the same accuracy.

The ELBO is the one I'd reach for by default: it's the cleanest
bias-for-compute trade, and it degrades gracefully when you can't afford
many samples.

## the bugs were most of the work

The idea was the easy part. Three bugs ate the rest of the time, and all
three were the silent kind that train fine and just learn the wrong thing:

- **An off-by-one in the AR logit shift.** Standard next-token alignment,
  wrong by one position at the block boundary, so the log-prob was scoring a
  shifted sequence. Quietly poisons every gradient.
- **A log-of-sum where the math wanted sum-of-logs** in the bound (it had
  become an upper bound, an EUBO, with the wrong reduction). Jensen's
  inequality points the other way, so the "lower bound" wasn't one.
- **Reused mask seeds across iterations**, which correlated the estimates
  and shrank the effective sample size without telling you.

None of these throws. They just bias the estimate, and you only catch them
by deriving the quantity and checking the code computes that and not a
plausible neighbor. That's the real lesson of the project: in RL on top of an
approximate likelihood, the bugs hide inside numbers that look reasonable.

Fixed, block-GRPO with the ELBO estimator beat vanilla GRPO by about 10x on
tail reward over training (+0.158 vs +0.017), which is the regime that
actually matters, since the tail is where the hard prompts live.

## where this goes

The thing I keep circling is that all of this complexity exists to get a
usable gradient through an intractable likelihood. Evolution strategies
(Salimans et al. 2017,
[arxiv 1703.03864](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03864)) skip that entirely:
perturb the parameters, keep what scores better, never compute a log-prob at
all. For a model whose likelihood is this awkward, trading exact gradients
for black-box search might be the natural move, not a fallback. Probably
worth running ES head-to-head against block-GRPO on the same reward, one
variable at a time, and seeing which actually wins. Would love to look into
it.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/heartbeat.md -->
---
title: Building nexos.heartbeat: the infinite context problem
date: 2026-03-01
summary: An always-on AI twin doesn't have a context window problem, it has an infinite context problem. Information theory, the design space, and why our memory is a git repository.
---

An always-on assistant doesn't have a context window problem. It has an
infinite context problem, and that's a much deeper hole.

At nexos.ai my team has been building
[nexos.heartbeat](https://nexos.ai/heartbeat/), a digital AI twin: it
watches, learns, surfaces what matters, and acts before you ask. The pitch
is short. The problem behind it is one of the more interesting ones I've
worked on, and it isn't the one people expect.

## the infinite context problem

Context windows keep growing, and it's tempting to think the problem
dissolves on its own. It doesn't, because the input isn't a document, it's
a stream: every thread, meeting, draft, and half-decision, every day,
forever. No window holds an unbounded stream, and storage was never the hard
part (logs are cheap). The hard part is that at any moment almost none of the
past matters, and you don't know in advance which part does.

## memory is compression

Shannon's definition of information is surprise, and by that definition most
of the stream carries almost none: the signal is sparse. So the system has
to compress, and lossless doesn't save you, since a losslessly compressed
unbounded stream is still unbounded. Lossy compression forces a value
judgment. Rate-distortion theory says you can't even define it without
choosing what it costs to lose something, and that choice is the actual
product decision. The information bottleneck (Tishby, Pereira, Bialek, 1999)
frames it well: squeeze the stream through a bottleneck that keeps only what
predicts a chosen variable, and let that variable set the cost instead of
hand-picking one. For a twin the variable is action, not reconstruction, so
the question isn't "can it replay the past", it's "would it act differently
without this". Memory becomes a compressed belief state, sufficient
statistics for action (the information bottleneck is really just that idea,
the minimal sufficient statistic, generalized to lossy settings).

The counterintuitive consequence: a good twin is defined mostly by what it
ignores, and "gets smarter every day" literally means it compresses you
better. Compression and prediction are the same quantity seen from two
sides, so acting before you ask is just prediction crossing a confidence
threshold.

## the design space

The naive version is hierarchical RAG: embed everything, retrieve top-k,
summarize, repeat up a tree. It works until the part that matters today is
something you compressed away yesterday, because it didn't look important at
the time. Fixed summarization is lossy in a direction you chose too early.

What you actually want is memory you can revise: keep the compressed belief
state, but let new evidence reopen old conclusions. So the structure isn't a
summary, it's a versioned model of the user that updates as you learn.

## memory as a git repository

The design I keep coming back to is a repository of structured plain-text
files, versioned like code. State lives in readable files (who the user is,
what they're working on, what they care about), and every update is a diff
against that state. The history of diffs is the timeline: not a log of
events, but a log of how the model of the user changed.

This buys a few things almost for free. Concurrency: many processes can
propose updates, and you reconcile them like merges. Belief reconciliation:
a conflict between an old assumption and new evidence is a merge conflict,
and you resolve it explicitly instead of silently overwriting. Auditability:
you can read, in plain text, why the twin believes what it believes, and
roll back when it's wrong. Branches let you hold tentative models of the
user and only commit when they're confirmed.

[[demo:belief-repo]]

It's plain text because plain text is the most durable, inspectable,
mergeable format we have, and because a human (or another model) can read
the state and tell you it's wrong. A belief state you can't inspect is one
you can't correct.

## where this goes

The open question I find most interesting is when to act. A twin that acts
on every high-confidence prediction is exhausting; one that waits for
certainty is useless. The threshold is itself something you should learn per
person, from whether your past actions landed. That feedback loop, acting,
watching how it lands, updating the threshold, is probably the actual
product, and I'd love to write more about it once we've pushed on it
further.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/gpt2-ioi.md -->
---
title: GPT-2, IOI, and the sphex problem
date: 2025-05-21
summary: A wasp can look like it understands what it's doing right up until you move one thing. I poked at GPT-2's indirect-object circuit the same way, to see whether it understood the task or just had a routine that usually works.
---

The digger wasp Sphex drags its prey to the burrow, leaves it on the
threshold, goes in to check the nest, then comes back and hauls it in. Move
the prey a few inches while it's inside, and it drags it back to the
threshold and checks the nest *again*. You can run this loop forty times. The
behavior looks like understanding until you nudge one thing, and then it's
obviously a routine. Hofstadter named the trait sphexishness, and the
question I find it raises is: how would you tell the difference in a neural
network?

I spent some time on that with Buck Shlegeris at Redwood Research, poking at
GPT-2's indirect object identification (IOI) circuit. IOI is the task in
"When John and Mary went to the store, John gave a drink to ___", where the
model should say Mary. There's a celebrated paper that reverse-engineers the
exact circuit GPT-2 small uses for this
([Wang et al., "Interpretability in the Wild", 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00593)):
specific attention heads that find the duplicated name, suppress it, and copy
the other one. It's clean, and it's real. My question was the sphex one: does
that circuit understand IOI, or does it have a routine that usually works on
the sentences it was measured on?

## perturb it and watch

So I [perturbed the inputs](https://github.com/mariopenglee/GPT2IOInotebooks)
and watched what held, which is just behavioral analysis: vary the stimulus,
see when the behavior breaks. A few things fell out:

- **Name priors beat the syntax.** Swap in a rare name and the circuit
  wobbles. It isn't tracking "the non-repeated entity" abstractly so much as
  leaning on how name-like and frequent the tokens are. Common names win
  arguments they shouldn't.
- **GPT-2 small will happily pick the subject as its own object** ("Josh went
  with Josh"), a thing the GPT-Neo models mostly learned to punish. So the
  "circuit" is partly a smaller model's tolerance for a degenerate answer.
- **Add entities and it degrades by falling back on heuristics.** With four
  names in play GPT-Neo tracks the referent noticeably better than GPT-2, and
  when GPT-2 breaks it breaks toward proximity and repetition: grab the
  nearest plausible name, or the one it just saw. Routines, not reasoning.

[[demo:ioi-perturb]]

None of this says the circuit paper is wrong. The circuit is there. It says
the circuit implements something narrower than "identify the indirect
object", and you only see the gap by moving the prey.

## the layers you need

The way I think about it now is that interpretability has layers of
abstraction, and they map almost one-to-one onto how we study people.
Behavioral analysis is the psychology layer: treat the model as a black box,
vary inputs, characterize what it does. Circuit analysis is the cognitive
science layer: name the mechanism, the heads and the information flow.
Single-neuron work is the neuroscience layer: the wiring underneath.

My view is you need all three, and the cheap one comes first. Behavioral
analysis is fast and needs no internals, and it's the layer that tells you
*what to explain* before you spend weeks explaining it. Skip it and you risk
reverse-engineering a beautiful circuit for a behavior the model doesn't
robustly have. The expensive layers validate and localize; the cheap layer
keeps them honest.

The open thread I'd like to pull on is making the perturbation search
automatic: instead of hand-designing the nudge that breaks a circuit, search
for it, the adversarial-example version of the sphex test. If a circuit
survives a hard search for its breaking input, that's a much stronger claim
to understanding than surviving the sentences someone happened to try.
Probably worth building.


---

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/multitask-training.md -->
---
title: Does parameter sharing help? a multitask recommender experiment
date: 2025-05-10
summary: I built the same recommender four times to find out whether sharing parameters across tasks helps. It turned out the loss weighting mattered more than the sharing, which is a known and slightly annoying axis.
---

I built the same recommender four times to answer one question: does sharing
parameters across tasks actually help? The answer turned out to be "wrong
question." What moved the results wasn't whether the tasks shared a backbone,
it was how I weighted their two losses.
([code](https://github.com/mariopenglee/multitask-training-evaluation))

## the setup

Every user is a task. For each user-movie interaction the model predicts two
things at once: whether the user would engage with the item (binary
classification) and what rating they'd give it (regression). I built it both
ways that mattered at the time, classic Matrix Factorization and Neural
Collaborative Filtering, on the GroupLens MovieLens data, which covers the
linear and the deep end of collaborative filtering.

## the grid

Four configurations, crossing parameter sharing with loss weighting: sharing
on or off, weights at 0.99/0.1 or 0.5/0.5. The point was to separate two
questions that usually get conflated: does sharing help at all, and how much
of the outcome is really just the weighting in disguise. Control one
variable at a time.

## what I took away

The clean lesson wasn't a winning configuration, it was how far the answer
moved when the weights moved. With the wrong balance the "transfer" turns
into plain interference, one head quietly eating the other. So my view is
that multitask learning isn't a free lunch, it's a coupling knob, and the
weighting is as much a part of the architecture as the shared layers.

[[demo:loss-weighting]]

That's not just my MovieLens result. The weighting matters so much that a
whole line of work tries to stop hand-tuning it: Kendall et al. learn the
per-task weights from each task's uncertainty instead of setting them, and Yu
et al.'s PCGrad attacks the interference one level down, projecting away the
part of one task's gradient that conflicts with another's. Different fixes,
same underlying problem I ran into, that two objectives sharing a network are
coupled whether you like it or not.

The question, when does sharing between objectives help and when does it
hurt, has been one of the more durable ones I've worked on. It shows up in
adapters, in multi-objective reward models, basically anywhere one network
serves several masters. This was just the first time I measured it directly.

<!-- https://mariopenglee.com/blog/hello.md -->
---
title: Starting a blog
date: 2025-05-01
summary: Why this page exists, and what to expect.
---

I keep having half-thoughts about the things I build that don't fit in a
commit message or a paper, and then I lose them. This page is where they go
from now on: short notes on what I'm building and thinking about, written
more often than I'd manage without somewhere to put them.

## what to expect

Mostly AI engineering, with detours into linguistics, psychology, and
safety, plus some higher-level theory and math. Some posts will be long,
most will be short.

## why a terminal

Because why not. No hero images, no parallax, just text, the way I actually
work:

[[demo:terminal-typing]]

> Make technology accessible, inclusive, and safe for everyone.

That's the throughline. Thanks for reading, see you in the next one.
